essay_text: Some people believe cities should spend more money on public transport than on roads. I agree because reliable buses and trains move more people while using less space. First, a frequent network gives workers a practical alternative to private cars. This reduces congestion and also helps people who cannot afford a vehicle. For example, one full metro train can replace hundreds of cars during the morning rush. Second, road expansion often creates only temporary relief because easier driving encourages more journeys. Investment in dedicated bus lanes, safe stations and integrated tickets has a longer effect. Roads still require maintenance, particularly for emergency services and freight, but constructing additional urban motorways should not be the priority. In conclusion, cities gain cleaner air, fairer access and more efficient travel when most new transport funding is directed to public systems.

There is an ongoing debate about whether university education ought to be free for everyone. Although universal provision appears equitable, I believe public funding should be targeted. Removing all fees would undoubtedly widen participation, especially for capable students from low-income households. Society would also benefit from a larger pool of doctors, engineers and teachers. Nevertheless, affluent families can contribute without sacrificing essential needs, and governments face competing demands for healthcare and primary education. A blanket subsidy may therefore transfer scarce public money to people who require no assistance. A more sustainable model would combine income-tested grants with loans whose repayments begin only after graduates reach a reasonable salary. Courses linked to serious labour shortages could receive additional support. This approach preserves access while sharing costs according to ability to pay. Overall, higher education should be affordable to every qualified applicant, but affordability does not require the state to pay the entire bill for every student.

The claim that economic growth invariably improves happiness is attractive but incomplete. Rising incomes can transform well-being where households lack food, secure housing or medical care; in such circumstances, additional resources remove immediate sources of distress. Beyond that threshold, however, the distribution and quality of growth matter as much as its scale. Longer working hours, polluted neighbourhoods and insecure employment may accompany a larger economy while leaving daily life worse. Moreover, gains concentrated among a small minority can intensify social comparison and distrust. Governments should consequently judge progress through several measures, including health, leisure, environmental quality and reported life satisfaction, rather than treating gross domestic product as a complete scorecard. None of this makes growth irrelevant: it finances public services and creates opportunities. It does mean that growth is a tool, not the final objective. Policies succeed when prosperity is broadly shared and converted into healthier, safer and more autonomous lives.
